Snowball Earth. The hypothesis that our planet experienced episodes of near-total glaciation during the Proterozoic eon, when ice sheets extended all the way to the equator and covered the entire ocean surface. These extreme glacial events, lasting millions of years, were terminated by greenhouse warming from accumulated volcanic carbon dioxide. The Snowball Earth concept revolutionized our understanding of Earth's climate extremes and the resilience of life in the most hostile conditions imaginable.

These events occurred primarily during the Neoproterozoic Era, roughly between 850 and 635 million years ago, with at least two or three major glaciation episodes. Evidence for this extreme glaciation includes glacial deposits called tillites found at equatorial latitudes, dropstones—glacially transported rocks—embedded in marine sediments, and carbon isotope anomalies that indicate sharply reduced photosynthesis.

A global ice cover would reflect nearly all sunlight due to its high albedo, creating a runaway ice-albedo feedback that perpetuates freezing even at the equator. The Snowball Earth episodes likely ended when volcanic emissions accumulated sufficient carbon dioxide to trigger a strong greenhouse effect, warming the planet rapidly. The transition from glaciation to rapid warming would have created extreme environmental stress, yet evidence suggests life not only survived but actually radiated shortly afterward, giving rise to complex multicellular organisms.

This hypothesis explains the abrupt transition between the Proterozoic and Cambrian periods and the so-called Cambrian explosion of body plans. Some researchers propose Slush ball variants where thin equatorial ice allowed some photosynthesis, reducing the severity but maintaining the fundamental model. The hypothesis was controversial but is now supported by geological evidence including iron oxide deposits formed under anoxic conditions beneath global ice sheets. Metabolic innovations—perhaps chemosynthetic bacteria thriving in ice-free refugia—may have enabled the rapid diversification of eukaryotic life following deglaciation.
